Module 06 / Physics 2

Capacitors: first decide what stays fixed

Plate geometry, dielectrics, charge, energy, and complete networks.

Topics in this module
Derive parallel-plate capacitanceDielectrics: connected versus disconnected batteryDerive all three energy expressionsNetworks: derive series and parallel rulesDerive capacitance with the charge, geometry, and units visibleRestore every capacitor in the source networksEnergy, dielectric insertion, and capacitor applicationsSituational problems: choose the law, then solve

A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between conductors. Its plates carry +Q and −Q. In C=QVC = \frac{Q}{V}C=VQ​, Q is the magnitude on ONE plate, not the algebraic total charge of the pair. One farad is one coulomb per volt. Use μF=10−6 F\mathrm{\mu F} = 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}μF=10−6F, nF=10−9 F\mathrm{nF} = 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F}nF=10−9F, and pF=10−12 F\mathrm{pF} = 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F}pF=10−12F.

C=Q/V,Q=CV,V=Q/C.C=Q/V,\quad Q=CV,\quad V=Q/C.C=Q/V,Q=CV,V=Q/C.

For a linear ideal capacitor, geometry and dielectric determine C. A larger Q does not automatically mean a larger C: the applied voltage can increase in the same proportion. Capacitive keyboard keys exploit smaller separation increasing capacitance.

Derive parallel-plate capacitance

For large parallel plates with edge effects neglected, σ=QA\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}σ=AQ​ and E=σεE = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}E=εσ​. The approximately uniform gap field gives V=EdV = EdV=Ed. Substitute:

V=QdϵA⇒C=QV=ϵAd=κϵ0Ad.V=\frac{Qd}{\epsilon A}\Rightarrow C=\frac QV=\frac{\epsilon A}{d}=\frac{\kappa\epsilon_0 A}{d}.V=ϵAQd​⇒C=VQ​=dϵA​=dκϵ0​A​.

Here ε0≈8.85×10−12 Fm\varepsilon_{0} \approx 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\,\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{m}}ε0​≈8.85×10−12mF​ and κ\kappaκ is a dimensionless dielectric constant. Rearrangements are A=Cd(κε0)A = \frac{Cd}{\left( \kappa \varepsilon_{0} \right)}A=(κε0​)Cd​, d=κε0ACd = \frac{\kappa \varepsilon_{0} A}{C}d=Cκε0​A​, κ=Cd(ε0A)\kappa = \frac{Cd}{\left( \varepsilon_{0} A \right)}κ=(ε0​A)Cd​. The parallel-plate model needs plate dimensions much larger than gap d. Do not use the same equation for arbitrary conductor shapes.

Worked example — primary p. 14. C=1.0 FC = 1.0\,\mathrm{F}C=1.0F, d=1.0 mmd = 1.0\,\mathrm{mm}d=1.0mm in vacuum gives A=1×0.001(8.85×10−12)=1.13×108 m2A = \frac{1 \times 0.001}{\left( 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \right)} = 1.13 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}^{2}A=(8.85×10−12)1×0.001​=1.13×108m2. A missing milli prefix changes the answer by 1000.

Worked example — primary p. 14. A=2.0 m2A = 2.0\,\mathrm{m}^{2}A=2.0m2, d=5.0 mmd = 5.0\,\mathrm{mm}d=5.0mm, and V=10,000 VV = 10{,}000\,\mathrm{V}V=10,000V give C=3.54×10−9 F=0.00354 μFC = 3.54 \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F} = 0.00354\,\mathrm{\mu F}C=3.54×10−9F=0.00354μF, Q=35.4 μCQ = 35.4\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q=35.4μC, and E=2.0×106 VmE = 2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{m}}E=2.0×106mV​. Check Q=CVQ = CVQ=CV and V=EdV = EdV=Ed independently.

Dielectrics: connected versus disconnected battery

A dielectric polarizes and increases capacitance when it fills the gap: Cnew=κColdC_{\mathrm{new}} = \kappa C_{\mathrm{old}}Cnew​=κCold​. It can mechanically separate plates and permit greater voltage before breakdown, depending on the material and conditions.

Quantity Battery stays connected Battery is disconnected, ideal isolated capacitor
Voltage Fixed by ideal battery Divides by κ\kappaκ
Free charge magnitude Multiplies by κ\kappaκ Fixed
Capacitance Multiplies by κ\kappaκ Multiplies by κ\kappaκ
Field in fully filled fixed gap Fixed Divides by κ\kappaκ
Stored energy Multiplies by κ\kappaκ Divides by κ\kappaκ

Derive these changes. Start with Q=CVQ = CVQ=CV. Fix V in the connected case or Q in the isolated case. Then use U=CV22U = \frac{CV^{2}}{2}U=2CV2​ or Q2(2 C)\frac{Q^{2}}{\left( 2\,\mathrm{C} \right)}(2C)Q2​. The connected capacitor can gain stored energy because the battery exchanges energy and charge. The isolated capacitor's energy decrease can become mechanical work during dielectric insertion.

Extensions — partial dielectric geometry. Two materials occupying side-by-side area fractions share the voltage, so C=ε0(κ1A1+κ2A2)dC = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} \left( \kappa_{1} A_{1} + \kappa_{2} A_{2} \right)}{d}C=dε0​(κ1​A1​+κ2​A2​)​. Layers stacked across the gap share the series charge, so 1C=d1(κ1ε0A)+d2(κ2ε0A)\frac{1}{C} = \frac{d_{1}}{\left( \kappa_{1} \varepsilon_{0} A \right)} + \frac{d_{2}}{\left( \kappa_{2} \varepsilon_{0} A \right)}C1​=(κ1​ε0​A)d1​​+(κ2​ε0​A)d2​​. Use the geometry to choose the connection model.

Derive all three energy expressions

The voltage rises while charging. An additional dq requires work dU=V(q)dq=(qC)dqdU = V \left( q \right) dq = \left( \frac{q}{C} \right) dqdU=V(q)dq=(Cq​)dq. Integrate from zero to Q:

U=∫0QqC dq=Q22C=12QV=12CV2.U=\int_0^Q\frac qC\,dq=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12QV=\frac12CV^2.U=∫0Q​Cq​dq=2CQ2​=21​QV=21​CV2.

Multiplying the FINAL voltage by the entire charge gives QV, twice the stored energy. A linear voltage rise has average charging voltage V2\frac{V}{2}2V​. Rearranging gives V=(2UC)V = \sqrt{\left( \frac{2 U}{C} \right)}V=(C2U​)​, C=2UV2C = \frac{2 U}{V^{2}}C=V22U​, or Q=(2CU)Q = \sqrt{\left( 2 CU \right)}Q=(2CU)​, with magnitudes and physically positive C.

Worked example — primary p. 16. C=5.80 μFC = 5.80\,\mathrm{\mu F}C=5.80μF and V=400 VV = 400\,\mathrm{V}V=400V give U=0.5(5.80×10−6)(4002)=0.464 JU = 0.5 \left( 5.80 \times 10^{-6} \right) \left( 400^{2} \right) = 0.464\,\mathrm{J}U=0.5(5.80×10−6)(4002)=0.464J. The answer fixes the exponent obscured in some PDF text extraction. A 5.0 μF5.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}5.0μF capacitor at 1.5 V1.5\,\mathrm{V}1.5V has Q=7.5 μCQ = 7.5\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q=7.5μC.

Substitute C=εAdC = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}C=dεA​ and V=EdV = EdV=Ed: U=εE2Ad2U = \frac{\varepsilon E^{2} Ad}{2}U=2εE2Ad​. Divide by gap volume Ad to derive field-energy density u=εE22u = \frac{\varepsilon E^{2}}{2}u=2εE2​ for a linear material.

Networks: derive series and parallel rules

Parallel branches share the SAME two nodes. Their voltages are equal and terminal charges add: Qtot=∑CiVQ_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum C_{i} VQtot​=∑Ci​V. Thus Ceq=∑CiC_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum C_{i}Ceq​=∑Ci​. Series capacitors in an initially uncharged isolated-intermediate-node chain carry equal charge magnitude. Their voltage drops add: Vtot=Q∑(1Ci)V_{\mathrm{tot}} = Q\sum \left( \frac{1}{C_{i}} \right)Vtot​=Q∑(Ci​1​), so 1Ceq=∑i1Ci\frac1{C_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\sum_i\frac1{C_i}Ceq​1​=∑i​Ci​1​.

For two series capacitors, Ceq=C1C2(C1+C2)C_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{C_{1} C_{2}}{\left( C_{1} + C_{2} \right)}Ceq​=(C1​+C2​)C1​C2​​. Solving for an unknown gives C2=CeqC1(C1−Ceq)C_{2} = \frac{C_{\mathrm{eq}}C_{1}}{\left( C_{1} - C_{\mathrm{eq}} \right)}C2​=(C1​−Ceq​)Ceq​C1​​, requiring C1>Ceq>0C_{1} > C_{\mathrm{eq}} > 0C1​>Ceq​>0. In parallel, C2=Ceq−C1>0C_{2} = C_{\mathrm{eq}} - C_{1} > 0C2​=Ceq​−C1​>0. Series equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest element; parallel equivalent capacitance exceeds each positive element.

Worked example — primary p. 24. Connect 6 μF6\,\mathrm{\mu F}6μF and 3 μF3\,\mathrm{\mu F}3μF to 18 V18\,\mathrm{V}18V. Series: Ceq=2 μFC_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}Ceq​=2μF, Qeach=36 μCQ_{\mathrm{each}} = 36\,\mathrm{\mu C}Qeach​=36μC, V6=6 VV_{6} = 6\,\mathrm{V}V6​=6V, V3=12 VV_{3} = 12\,\mathrm{V}V3​=12V. Parallel: Ceq=9 μFC_{\mathrm{eq}} = 9\,\mathrm{\mu F}Ceq​=9μF, Veach=18 VV_{\mathrm{each}} = 18\,\mathrm{V}Veach​=18V, Q6=108 μCQ_{6} = 108\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q6​=108μC, Q3=54 μCQ_{3} = 54\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q3​=54μC. The smaller SERIES capacitor has the larger voltage because its charge magnitude is the same.

For a mixed network, label nodes before reducing it. Two nearby symbols are not necessarily parallel. Reduce a valid group, record its equivalent value, solve the terminal circuit, and then work backward. Use the original group’s shared Q or shared V to recover each element. Check ΣVi for series groups and ΣQi for parallel groups.

Worked extension — reduce, then restore the branches. Put 2 μF2\,\mathrm{\mu F}2μF and 4 μF4\,\mathrm{\mu F}4μF in parallel. Connect that group in series with 3 μF3\,\mathrm{\mu F}3μF across 12 V12\,\mathrm{V}12V. The parallel group is 6 μF6\,\mathrm{\mu F}6μF. Its series equivalent with 3 μF3\,\mathrm{\mu F}3μF is (6×3)(6+3)=2 μF\frac{\left( 6 \times 3 \right)}{\left( 6 + 3 \right)} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}(6+3)(6×3)​=2μF. The source transfers Q=2×12=24 μCQ = 2 \times 12 = 24\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q=2×12=24μC to each series unit.

The 6 μF6\,\mathrm{\mu F}6μF group has voltage 246=4 V\frac{24}{6} = 4\,\mathrm{V}624​=4V. The 3 μF3\,\mathrm{\mu F}3μF capacitor has voltage 243=8 V\frac{24}{3} = 8\,\mathrm{V}324​=8V. Both parallel capacitors share 4 V4\,\mathrm{V}4V, so their charges are 8 μC8\,\mathrm{\mu C}8μC and 16 μC16\,\mathrm{\mu C}16μC. Their sum is the group's 24 μC24\,\mathrm{\mu C}24μC. Check energy: 12(2 μF)(122)=144 μJ\tfrac{1}{2} \left( 2\,\mathrm{\mu F} \right) \left( 12^{2} \right) = 144\,\mathrm{\mu J}21​(2μF)(122)=144μJ. The individual energies are 16, 32, and 96 μJ96\,\mathrm{\mu J}96μJ, which also sum to 144 μJ144\,\mathrm{\mu J}144μJ. A single equivalent capacitance alone does not reveal every branch voltage.

Charge-sharing extension. Disconnect two capacitors from their supplies and join their positive plates together. With no leakage, Vf=(C1V1+C2V2)(C1+C2)V_{f} = \frac{\left( C_{1} V_{1} + C_{2} V_{2} \right)}{\left( C_{1} + C_{2} \right)}Vf​=(C1​+C2​)(C1​V1​+C2​V2​)​. Reverse one capacitor's polarity by using a negative signed initial voltage. Final energy need not equal the sum of initial capacitor energies; the connection can dissipate energy. Charge conservation does not imply capacitor-energy conservation.

For C1=2 μFC_{1} = 2\,\mathrm{\mu F}C1​=2μF at 12 V12\,\mathrm{V}12V and C2=4 μFC_{2} = 4\,\mathrm{\mu F}C2​=4μF at 0 V0\,\mathrm{V}0V, Vf=4 VV_{f} = 4\,\mathrm{V}Vf​=4V. Initial stored energy is 144 μJ144\,\mathrm{\mu J}144μJ; final energy is 48 μJ48\,\mathrm{\mu J}48μJ. The difference, 96 μJ96\,\mathrm{\mu J}96μJ, leaves the capacitor fields during the transient. Real connections transfer it through resistance, radiation, or other losses. An ideal zero-resistance instantaneous connection is not a complete transient model.

Derive capacitance with the charge, geometry, and units visible

Derivation∴

From the plate fields to C=εAdC = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}C=dεA​

Sources: Primary pp. 7–13; companion pp. 1–4. Use large parallel plates, a uniform linear dielectric, and negligible edge effects.

  1. Write the free surface-charge density as σ=QA\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}σ=AQ​.
  2. Add the two ideal plate fields. The gap field is E=σεE = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}E=εσ​, not σ(2ε)\frac{\sigma}{\left( 2 \varepsilon \right)}(2ε)σ​.
  3. Use the uniform-gap potential difference magnitude V=EdV = EdV=Ed.
  4. Substitute σ=QA\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}σ=AQ​ to obtain V=Qd(εA)V = \frac{Qd}{\left( \varepsilon A \right)}V=(εA)Qd​.
  5. Divide charge by voltage: C=QV=εAdC = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}C=VQ​=dεA​.

Unit check. εAd\frac{\varepsilon A}{d}dεA​ has units (Fm)(m2)m=F\frac{\left( \frac{F}{m} \right) \left( m^{2} \right)}{m} = Fm(mF​)(m2)​=F. The dielectric constant κ=εε0\kappa = \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_{0}}κ=ε0​ε​ has no unit. Do not confuse κ\kappaκ with Coulomb's constant k.

The table gives κ=1\kappa = 1κ=1 for vacuum and about 1.00059 for air at 1 atm1\,\mathrm{atm}1atm. The usual classroom approximation uses air ≈ vacuum. Listed examples include Teflon 2.1, polyethylene 2.25, glass 5–10, and water 80.4. Capacitance depends on both geometry and the dielectric, not geometry alone when materials change.

Energy, dielectric insertion, and capacitor applications

Worked solution↳

Evaluate the source energy and charge questions

Source: Primary p. 16.

  1. Convert C=5.80 μFC = 5.80\,\mathrm{\mu F}C=5.80μF to 5.80×10−6 F5.80 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{F}5.80×10−6F and use V=400 VV = 400\,\mathrm{V}V=400V.
  2. Calculate U=12CV2=12(5.80×10−6)(4002)=0.464 J\begin{aligned}U &= \tfrac{1}{2} CV^{2} \\&= \tfrac{1}{2} \left( 5.80 \times 10^{-6} \right) \left( 400^{2} \right) \\&= 0.464\,\mathrm{J}\end{aligned}U​=21​CV2=21​(5.80×10−6)(4002)=0.464J​
  3. For the separate 5.0 μF5.0\,\mathrm{\mu F}5.0μF, 1.5 V1.5\,\mathrm{V}1.5V problem, use Q=CV=7.5 μCQ = CV = 7.5\,\mathrm{\mu C}Q=CV=7.5μC.

Check. Squaring the voltage squares its factor of ten. The first problem's plate separation is not needed once C and V are already supplied.

Derivation∴

Battery work and stored energy during dielectric insertion

This is a labeled extension. Initially C0C_{0}C0​ and V0V_{0}V0​ describe the capacitor. Insert a dielectric of constant κ\kappaκ quasistatically into the entire fixed gap, while an ideal battery stays connected.

  1. Find ΔQ=(κ−1)C0V0\Delta Q = \left( \kappa - 1 \right) C_{0} V_{0}ΔQ=(κ−1)C0​V0​ from Q=CVQ = CVQ=CV.
  2. Calculate battery energy supplied: Wbattery=V0ΔQ=(κ−1)C0V02W_{\mathrm{battery}} = V_{0} \Delta Q = \left( \kappa - 1 \right) C_{0} V_{0}^{2}Wbattery​=V0​ΔQ=(κ−1)C0​V02​.
  3. Calculate the increase in stored field energy: ΔU=12(κ−1)C0V02\Delta U = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( \kappa - 1 \right) C_{0} V_{0}^{2}ΔU=21​(κ−1)C0​V02​.
  4. Under the ideal loss-free quasistatic model, the remaining half leaves as mechanical work by the field on the dielectric.
Wfield,mech=Wbattery−ΔU=12(κ−1)C0V02.W_{field,mech}=W_{battery}-\Delta U =\frac12(\kappa-1)C_0V_0^2.Wfield,mech​=Wbattery​−ΔU=21​(κ−1)C0​V02​.

For an isolated capacitor, the battery supplies no energy. Its field energy decreases from Q02(2C0)\frac{Q_{0}^{2}}{\left( 2 C_{0} \right)}(2C0​)Q02​​ to Q02(2κC0)\frac{Q_{0}^{2}}{\left( 2 \kappa C_{0} \right)}(2κC0​)Q02​​. The decrease can become mechanical work. State the electrical connection before applying energy conservation.

Applications — primary p. 26. A camera flash stores energy over a longer charging interval and releases it over a shorter interval. The same energy released in less time gives greater average power, Pavg=ΔUΔtP_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\Delta U}{\Delta t}Pavg​=ΔtΔU​. Capacitors also smooth changing supply voltages and provide brief charge pulses. Their circuit role depends on the connection, not merely the presence of a capacitor symbol.

Situational problems: choose the law, then solve

These added practice problems apply the module concepts. They are not copied examination questions. Keep the stated assumptions when you use each result.

Situation 1: Dielectric with the battery removed

An ideal charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery. A dielectric completely fills its unchanged gap, increasing capacitance by a factor κ>1. Ignore leakage. Which comparison is correct?

  1. Identify the boundary condition. Disconnection and negligible leakage hold the free plate charge fixed.

  2. Use the new capacitance.

C′=κCC'=\kappa CC′=κC
  1. Derive voltage and energy ratios.
V′=QκC=Vκ,U′=Q22κC=UκV'=\frac Q{\kappa C}=\frac V\kappa,\quad U'=\frac{Q^2}{2\kappa C}=\frac U\kappaV′=κCQ​=κV​,U′=2κCQ2​=κU​
  1. Account for energy. Field energy can decrease while the electric force does mechanical work on the inserted material.

Answer: QQQ stays fixed, while VVV and stored field energy each divide by κ\kappaκ.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • VVV stays fixed and charge multiplies by κ\kappaκ. — That describes a connected ideal voltage source, not this isolated capacitor.
  • Charge and energy both stay fixed. — Charge conservation does not imply fixed field energy.
  • Energy multiplies by κ\kappaκ because capacitance increases. — That uses a fixed-voltage energy comparison despite the disconnected battery.

Situation 2: Why connected insertion needs the source

A dielectric is inserted quasistatically while an ideal battery stays connected to a capacitor at fixed voltage. Capacitance increases. How can the capacitor’s stored energy increase while the dielectric is pulled inward?

  1. Use the fixed-voltage condition.
Q=CV,U=12CV2Q=CV,\qquad U=\tfrac12CV^2Q=CV,U=21​CV2
  1. Compare source work for a change in capacitance.
Wbattery=VΔQ=V2ΔCW_{\mathrm{battery}}=V\Delta Q=V^2\Delta CWbattery​=VΔQ=V2ΔC
  1. Compare the stored-energy increase.
ΔU=12V2ΔC\Delta U=\tfrac12V^2\Delta CΔU=21​V2ΔC
  1. Identify the remaining energy transfer. In the ideal quasistatic model, the remaining half can appear as mechanical work. A field-only comparison omits this source contribution.

Answer: The battery supplies energy; the capacitor field is not an isolated energy system.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Energy conservation fails for dielectrics. — Include the source and mechanical work before testing conservation.
  • The plate charge must stay fixed because the geometry is fixed. — A connected battery can transfer charge as capacitance changes.
  • A rise in capacitor energy proves the force pushes the dielectric outward. — That inference omits the battery energy exchange.

Situation 3: Parallel capacitors after disconnection

A charged capacitor is disconnected from its source, then connected in parallel with an initially uncharged equal capacitor, with corresponding plates joined. A small connection resistance allows equilibrium. Which statement is correct?

  1. Conserve charge on the joined positive node.
CV0=(C+C)VfCV_0=(C+C)V_fCV0​=(C+C)Vf​
  1. Find the shared final voltage.
Vf=V0/2V_f=V_0/2Vf​=V0​/2
  1. Compare field energies.
Ui=12CV02,Uf=12(2C)(V0/2)2=Ui/2U_i=\tfrac12CV_0^2,\quad U_f=\tfrac12(2C)(V_0/2)^2=U_i/2Ui​=21​CV02​,Uf​=21​(2C)(V0​/2)2=Ui​/2
  1. Complete the energy account. The finite connection dissipates energy during the transient. Conserving charge does not require conserving field energy alone.

Answer: Charge is conserved, the final voltage halves, and some initial field energy is dissipated.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Both charge and capacitor field energy remain entirely in the final electric field. — The final shared voltage gives a lower total field energy.
  • The final voltage remains equal to the original voltage. — No connected battery holds it there.
  • The initially uncharged capacitor cannot acquire charge. — The joined conductors allow redistribution.

Situation 4: Series charge and component voltage

Two initially uncharged capacitors are placed in series across a battery with an initially neutral isolated intermediate node. One capacitor has three times the other’s capacitance. Which comparison is correct?

  1. Use the intermediate-node condition. Opposite induced charges on the two inner plates have equal magnitudes.

  2. Apply the component relation.

V1=Q/C1,V2=Q/C2V_1=Q/C_1,\qquad V_2=Q/C_2V1​=Q/C1​,V2​=Q/C2​
  1. Take the ratio.
VsmallVlarge=ClargeCsmall=3\frac{V_{\mathrm{small}}}{V_{\mathrm{large}}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{large}}}{C_{\mathrm{small}}}=3Vlarge​Vsmall​​=Csmall​Clarge​​=3
  1. Distinguish parallel. Parallel connections fix common voltage instead of common series charge.

Answer: They have equal charge magnitudes; the smaller capacitor has three times the voltage.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • They have equal voltages; the larger has three times the charge. — That is the parallel condition.
  • The larger capacitor must have the larger voltage. — Voltage is inversely proportional to capacitance at the common series charge.
  • Their equivalent capacitance exceeds the larger component. — A positive series equivalent is smaller than the smallest component.

Situation 5: Separating isolated capacitor plates

An ideal parallel-plate capacitor is charged and isolated. Its plate gap doubles while overlap area and permittivity remain fixed. Ignore fringing and leakage. Which result follows?

  1. Change the geometry.
C=ϵA/d⟹C′=C/2C=\epsilon A/d\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C'=C/2C=ϵA/d⟹C′=C/2
  1. Hold charge fixed.
V′=Q/C′=2VV'=Q/C'=2VV′=Q/C′=2V
  1. Use the fixed-charge energy form.
U′=Q2/(2C′)=2UU'=Q^2/(2C')=2UU′=Q2/(2C′)=2U
  1. Check the energy transfer. The external agent’s positive separation work increases stored field energy.

Answer: Capacitance halves, voltage doubles, and field energy doubles.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Capacitance doubles because the gap increases. — Capacitance is inversely proportional to the gap.
  • Voltage stays fixed because it was once connected to a battery. — A removed battery no longer enforces voltage.
  • Energy halves because capacitance halves. — That energy scaling would require fixed voltage, not fixed charge.

Situation 6: Recovering a series component’s energy

Initially uncharged capacitors 3.0 μF and 6.0 μF are in series across 12 V, with a neutral isolated middle node. Find the energy stored in the 3.0 μF capacitor.

  1. Reduce the series pair.
Ceq=3(6)3+6=2 μFC_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{3(6)}{3+6}=2\,\mu\mathrm FCeq​=3+63(6)​=2μF
  1. Find common charge.
Q=CeqV=2(12)=24 μCQ=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=2(12)=24\,\mu\mathrm CQ=Ceq​V=2(12)=24μC
  1. Recover the small capacitor’s voltage.
V3=Q/C3=24/3=8 VV_3=Q/C_3=24/3=8\,\mathrm VV3​=Q/C3​=24/3=8V
  1. Calculate that component’s energy. The 6 μF component has the remaining 4 V, so the recovered voltages add to 12 V.
U3=12(3.0×10−6)(8)2U_3=\tfrac12(3.0\times10^{-6})(8)^2U3​=21​(3.0×10−6)(8)2
  1. State the result.
9.6×10−5 J9.6\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J9.6×10−5J

Answer: 9.6×10−5 J9.6\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J9.6×10−5J

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 2.16×10−4 J2.16\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J2.16×10−4J — This incorrectly puts the full 12 V across the 3 μF component.
  • 4.8×10−5 J4.8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J4.8×10−5J — The component energy includes one half, but its actual voltage must first be found.
  • 1.44×10−4 J1.44\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J1.44×10−4J — This is the total energy of the series combination.

Situation 7: Isolated dielectric insertion

A 2.0 μF capacitor is charged to 10 V and disconnected. An ideal dielectric of κ=3\kappa=3κ=3 fully fills the unchanged gap without leakage. Find the final stored energy.

  1. Find the charge before disconnection.
Q=(2.0×10−6)(10)=20 μCQ=(2.0\times10^{-6})(10)=20\,\mu\mathrm CQ=(2.0×10−6)(10)=20μC
  1. Apply the dielectric change.
C′=3C=6.0 μFC'=3C=6.0\,\mu\mathrm FC′=3C=6.0μF
  1. Hold charge fixed.
U′=Q22C′=(20×10−6)22(6.0×10−6)U'=\frac{Q^2}{2C'}=\frac{(20\times10^{-6})^2}{2(6.0\times10^{-6})}U′=2C′Q2​=2(6.0×10−6)(20×10−6)2​

  1. Check the comparison. The initial energy is 100 μJ. Dividing by κ=3\kappa=3κ=3 gives the final field energy.

  2. State the result.

3.33333×10−5 J3.33333\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J3.33333×10−5J

Answer: 3.33333×10−5 J3.33333\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J3.33333×10−5J

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 3×10−4 J3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J3×10−4J — This uses the connected fixed-voltage scaling.
  • 1×10−4 J1\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J1×10−4J — This assumes unchanged field energy despite the mechanical interaction.
  • 1.11111×10−5 J1.11111\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J1.11111×10−5J — This divides the energy by κ² rather than κ at fixed charge.

Situation 8: Battery work during dielectric insertion

An ideal battery keeps 12 V across an initially 2.0 μF capacitor. A dielectric increases its capacitance to 8.0 μF during quasistatic insertion. Find the energy supplied by the battery, not just the capacitor-energy change.

  1. Find the capacitance increase.
ΔC=(8.0−2.0) μF=6.0×10−6 F\Delta C=(8.0-2.0)\,\mu\mathrm F=6.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FΔC=(8.0−2.0)μF=6.0×10−6F
  1. Find charge delivered at fixed voltage.
ΔQ=VΔC=12(6.0×10−6)=72 μC\Delta Q=V\Delta C=12(6.0\times10^{-6})=72\,\mu\mathrm CΔQ=VΔC=12(6.0×10−6)=72μC
  1. Calculate source work.
Wbattery=VΔQ=12(72×10−6)W_{\mathrm{battery}}=V\Delta Q=12(72\times10^{-6})Wbattery​=VΔQ=12(72×10−6)
  1. Check the larger energy account. The rest can become mechanical work in the stated quasistatic idealization.
ΔU=12ΔCV2=432 μJ\Delta U=\tfrac12\Delta CV^2=432\,\mu\mathrm JΔU=21​ΔCV2=432μJ
  1. State the result.
8.64×10−4 J8.64\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J8.64×10−4J

Answer: 8.64×10−4 J8.64\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J8.64×10−4J

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 4.32×10−4 J4.32\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J4.32×10−4J — This is the capacitor’s stored-energy increase, half the ideal battery work for this process.
  • 0.001152 J0.001152\,\mathrm J0.001152J — This counts the full final CV² rather than the change in delivered charge.
  • 2.88×10−4 J2.88\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J2.88×10−4J — This omits the actual capacitance change.

Situation 9: Geometry change after isolation

An ideal parallel-plate capacitor has area 0.030 m², gap 1.2 mm, and dielectric constant κ=2\kappa=2κ=2. It is charged to 100 V and isolated. The gap then doubles while the dielectric still completely fills it and κ remains fixed. Find the final stored energy. Use ε0=8.85×10−12 F m−1\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}ε0​=8.85×10−12Fm−1.

  1. Convert the original gap.
d0=1.2×10−3 md_0=1.2\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm md0​=1.2×10−3m
  1. Find the initial capacitance.
C0=κϵ0Ad0=4.425×10−10 FC_0=\frac{\kappa\epsilon_0A}{d_0}=4.425\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm FC0​=d0​κϵ0​A​=4.425×10−10F
  1. Hold the isolated charge fixed as the gap doubles.
Cf=C0/2,Q=C0V0C_f=C_0/2,\qquad Q=C_0V_0Cf​=C0​/2,Q=C0​V0​
  1. Use the final capacitance with that fixed charge. The final energy is twice the initial energy. External work separates the attracting plates.
Uf=(C0V0)22(C0/2)=C0V02U_f=\frac{(C_0V_0)^2}{2(C_0/2)}=C_0V_0^2Uf​=2(C0​/2)(C0​V0​)2​=C0​V02​
  1. State the result.
4.425×10−6 J4.425\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J4.425×10−6J

Answer: 4.425×10−6 J4.425\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J4.425×10−6J

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 1.10625×10−6 J1.10625\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J1.10625×10−6J — This applies fixed-voltage scaling to an isolated capacitor.
  • 2.2125×10−6 J2.2125\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J2.2125×10−6J — This is the initial field energy.
  • 8.85×10−6 J8.85\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm J8.85×10−6J — This doubles the correct final energy again.

Situation 10: Unequally charged capacitors share charge

Isolated capacitors 2.0 μF at 10 V and 3.0 μF at 4 V are connected in parallel with corresponding positive plates joined. A small resistance allows equilibrium. Find the final common voltage.

  1. Find charge on the joined positive node.
Qtotal=(2)(10)+(3)(4)=32 μCQ_{\mathrm{total}}=(2)(10)+(3)(4)=32\,\mu\mathrm CQtotal​=(2)(10)+(3)(4)=32μC
  1. Find the final parallel capacitance.
Cf=2+3=5 μFC_f=2+3=5\,\mu\mathrm FCf​=2+3=5μF
  1. Divide conserved charge by final capacitance.
Vf=32/5=6.4 VV_f=32/5=6.4\,\mathrm VVf​=32/5=6.4V
  1. Check the energy difference. The transient dissipates 21.6 μJ; conserving charge alone does not keep all initial energy in the final electric field.
Ui=124 μJ,Uf=102.4 μJU_i=124\,\mu\mathrm J,\quad U_f=102.4\,\mu\mathrm JUi​=124μJ,Uf​=102.4μJ
  1. State the result.
6.4 V6.4\,\mathrm V6.4V

Answer: 6.4 V6.4\,\mathrm V6.4V

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 7 V7\,\mathrm V7V — This averages voltages without capacitance weighting.
  • 8 V8\,\mathrm V8V — Conserve the joined-node charge rather than selecting an arbitrary intermediate voltage.
  • 14 V14\,\mathrm V14V — Parallel connection does not add the original voltages.

Situation 11: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · Find the equivalent capacitance

An initially uncharged capacitor C1=3×10−6 FC_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC1​=3×10−6F connects in series with a parallel pair C2=2.0 μFC_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm FC2​=2.0μF and C3=4×10−6 FC_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC3​=4×10−6F. An ideal 12 V source connects across the complete network. The internal connecting node starts neutral. Use the final steady electrostatic state. Find the equivalent capacitance.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Combine the parallel pair first. The series branch charges have equal magnitudes; the parallel capacitors share voltage.

  2. Reduce the parallel pair.

Cp=C2+C3=6×10−6 FC_p=C_2+C_3=6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCp​=C2​+C3​=6×10−6F
  1. Reduce the remaining series pair.
Ceq=C1Cp/(C1+Cp)=2×10−6 FC_{\rm eq}=C_1C_p/(C_1+C_p)=2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCeq​=C1​Cp​/(C1​+Cp​)=2×10−6F
  1. Recover branch charge and voltage.
Q1=CeqV=2.4×10−5 C,Vp=Q1/Cp=4 VQ_1=C_{\rm eq}V=2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C,\quad V_p=Q_1/C_p=4\,\mathrm VQ1​=Ceq​V=2.4×10−5C,Vp​=Q1​/Cp​=4V
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
Ceq=3×10−6(6×10−6)9×10−6C_{\rm eq}=\frac{3\times10^{-6}(6\times10^{-6})}{9\times10^{-6}}Ceq​=9×10−63×10−6(6×10−6)​

  1. Check the physical result. The total series capacitance is below either of its two branch capacitances.

  2. State the result.

2×10−6 F2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F2×10−6F

Answer: 2×10−6 F2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F2×10−6F

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 9×10−6 F9\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F9×10−6F — This treats the whole network as parallel.
  • 9.23077×10−7 F9.23077\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm F9.23077×10−7F — This treats the parallel pair as series.
  • 6×10−6 F6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F6×10−6F — This omits the series capacitor.

Situation 12: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · Find the magnitude of charge on C1

An initially uncharged capacitor C1=3×10−6 FC_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC1​=3×10−6F connects in series with a parallel pair C2=2.0 μFC_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm FC2​=2.0μF and C3=4×10−6 FC_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC3​=4×10−6F. An ideal 12 V source connects across the complete network. The internal connecting node starts neutral. Use the final steady electrostatic state. Find the magnitude of charge on C1.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Combine the parallel pair first. The series branch charges have equal magnitudes; the parallel capacitors share voltage.

  2. Reduce the parallel pair.

Cp=C2+C3=6×10−6 FC_p=C_2+C_3=6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCp​=C2​+C3​=6×10−6F
  1. Reduce the remaining series pair.
Ceq=C1Cp/(C1+Cp)=2×10−6 FC_{\rm eq}=C_1C_p/(C_1+C_p)=2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCeq​=C1​Cp​/(C1​+Cp​)=2×10−6F
  1. Recover branch charge and voltage.
Q1=CeqV=2.4×10−5 C,Vp=Q1/Cp=4 VQ_1=C_{\rm eq}V=2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C,\quad V_p=Q_1/C_p=4\,\mathrm VQ1​=Ceq​V=2.4×10−5C,Vp​=Q1​/Cp​=4V
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
Q1=CeqV=2×10−6(12)Q_1=C_{\rm eq}V=2\times10^{-6}(12)Q1​=Ceq​V=2×10−6(12)

  1. Check the physical result. Equal series charge applies to C1 and the whole parallel branch, not separately to C2 and C3.

  2. State the result.

2.4×10−5 C2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C2.4×10−5C

Answer: 2.4×10−5 C2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C2.4×10−5C

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 3.6×10−5 C3.6\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C3.6×10−5C — C1 does not receive the full source voltage.
  • 7.2×10−5 C7.2\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C7.2×10−5C — The parallel pair does not receive the full source voltage.
  • 1.2×10−5 C1.2\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C1.2×10−5C — Series branch charge magnitudes are equal; source voltage is not split by halving the charge.

Situation 13: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · Find the voltage across C3

An initially uncharged capacitor C1=3×10−6 FC_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC1​=3×10−6F connects in series with a parallel pair C2=2.0 μFC_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm FC2​=2.0μF and C3=4×10−6 FC_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC3​=4×10−6F. An ideal 12 V source connects across the complete network. The internal connecting node starts neutral. Use the final steady electrostatic state. Find the voltage across C3.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Combine the parallel pair first. The series branch charges have equal magnitudes; the parallel capacitors share voltage.

  2. Reduce the parallel pair.

Cp=C2+C3=6×10−6 FC_p=C_2+C_3=6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCp​=C2​+C3​=6×10−6F
  1. Reduce the remaining series pair.
Ceq=C1Cp/(C1+Cp)=2×10−6 FC_{\rm eq}=C_1C_p/(C_1+C_p)=2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCeq​=C1​Cp​/(C1​+Cp​)=2×10−6F
  1. Recover branch charge and voltage.
Q1=CeqV=2.4×10−5 C,Vp=Q1/Cp=4 VQ_1=C_{\rm eq}V=2.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C,\quad V_p=Q_1/C_p=4\,\mathrm VQ1​=Ceq​V=2.4×10−5C,Vp​=Q1​/Cp​=4V
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
V3=Vp=Q1/(C2+C3)=4 VV_3=V_p=Q_1/(C_2+C_3)=4\,\mathrm VV3​=Vp​=Q1​/(C2​+C3​)=4V

  1. Check the physical result. C2 and C3 share the same parallel voltage.

  2. State the result.

4 V4\,\mathrm V4V

Answer: 4 V4\,\mathrm V4V

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 12 V12\,\mathrm V12V — The series capacitor takes part of the total voltage.
  • 8 V8\,\mathrm V8V — This gives the voltage across C1.
  • 6 V6\,\mathrm V6V — The whole branch charge is shared by C2 and C3.

Situation 14: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · Find the energy stored in C3 alone

An initially uncharged capacitor C1=3×10−6 FC_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC1​=3×10−6F connects in series with a parallel pair C2=2.0 μFC_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm FC2​=2.0μF and C3=4×10−6 FC_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC3​=4×10−6F. An ideal 12 V source connects across the complete network. The internal connecting node starts neutral. Use the final steady electrostatic state. Find the energy stored in C3 alone.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Combine the parallel pair first. The series branch charges have equal magnitudes; the parallel capacitors share voltage.

  2. Reduce the parallel pair.

Cp=C2+C3=6×10−6 FC_p=C_2+C_3=6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCp​=C2​+C3​=6×10−6F
  1. Reduce the remaining series pair.
Ceq=C1Cp/(C1+Cp)=2×10−6 FC_{\rm eq}=C_1C_p/(C_1+C_p)=2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCeq​=C1​Cp​/(C1​+Cp​)=2×10−6F
  1. Recover branch charge and voltage.

Situation 15: A series capacitor feeds a parallel pair · model check

An initially uncharged capacitor C1=3×10−6 FC_1=3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC1​=3×10−6F connects in series with a parallel pair C2=2.0 μFC_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm FC2​=2.0μF and C3=4×10−6 FC_3=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC3​=4×10−6F. Which equality applies to the two capacitors in the parallel pair?

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Combine the parallel pair first. The series branch charges have equal magnitudes; the parallel capacitors share voltage.

  2. Reduce the parallel pair.

Cp=C2+C3=6×10−6 FC_p=C_2+C_3=6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FCp​=C2​+C3​=6×10−6F
  1. Reduce the remaining series pair.

Answer: Their voltages are equal; their charges need not be equal.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Their charges must equal the full C1 charge separately. — Their charges sum to the charge magnitude of the parallel branch.

  • Their capacitances become equal after charging. — Capacitance is set by geometry and material.

Situation 30: A dielectric covers only part of the area · model check

A parallel-plate capacitor has area 0.04 m² and gap 0.0015 m. A dielectric of relative permittivity 4 completely fills the gap over fraction 0.6 of the plate area. The remaining area contains vacuum. An ideal 120 V source remains connected. Ignore fringing. Use ε0=8.85×10−12 F m−1\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}ε0​=8.85×10−12Fm−1. Why are these two regions parallel rather than series?

  1. Identify what stays fixed. The side-by-side regions have the same plate voltage, so they form parallel capacitances.

  2. Calculate the vacuum reference capacitance.

C0=ε0A/d=2.36×10−10 FC_0=\varepsilon_0A/d=2.36\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm FC0​=ε0​A/d=2.36×10−10F
  1. Add the two area regions in parallel.
C=C0[(1−f)+κf]=6.608×10−10 FC=C_0[(1-f)+\kappa f]=6.608\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm FC=C0​[(1−f)+κf]=6.608×10−10F
  1. Apply the connected-source constraint.
V=constant,Q=CV,U=12CV2V=\text{constant},\quad Q=CV,\quad U=\tfrac12CV^2V=constant,Q=CV,U=21​CV2
  1. Apply the conclusion. A common pair of endpoint potentials defines parallel connection.

Answer: Both regions connect the same two plates and have the same potential difference.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Their dielectric constants are different. — Different material alone does not determine a series or parallel geometry.
  • The electric field crosses one region and then the other along the gap. — Here the regions lie side by side across plate area, not consecutively through the gap.

Situation 50: Connect oppositely charged capacitors · model check

Two isolated capacitors have C1=4×10−6 FC_1=4\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm FC1​=4×10−6F at 12 V and C2=2.0 μFC_2=2.0\,\mu\mathrm FC2​=2.0μF at 5 V. They connect in parallel with C1’s positive plate joined to C2’s negative plate. The other plates also join. A small resistance allows settling. Define the joined C1-positive node as the positive voltage reference. Why is it incorrect to conserve total capacitor field energy during this connection?

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Conserve signed charge on each joined node. Opposite initial polarities subtract; resistor heating accounts for lost field energy.

  2. Add signed charge on the reference node.

Qnode=C1V1−C2V2=3.8×10−5 CQ_{\rm node}=C_1V_1-C_2V_2=3.8\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm CQnode​=C1​V1​−C2​V2​=3.8×10−5C
  1. Use the final parallel capacitance.
Vf=Qnode/(C1+C2)=6.33333 VV_f=Q_{\rm node}/(C_1+C_2)=6.33333\,\mathrm VVf​=Qnode​/(C1​+C2​)=6.33333V
  1. Compare field energies.
Ui=12C1V12+12C2V22=3.13×10−4 J,Uf=12(C1+C2)Vf2=1.20333×10−4 J\begin{gathered}U_i=\tfrac12C_1V_1^2+\tfrac12C_2V_2^2=3.13\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J,\\U_f=\tfrac12(C_1+C_2)V_f^2=1.20333\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J\end{gathered}Ui​=21​C1​V12​+21​C2​V22​=3.13×10−4J,Uf​=21​(C1​+C2​)Vf2​=1.20333×10−4J​

Answer: The transient current dissipates energy in the settling resistance.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Charge conservation fails during a transient. — Charge still cannot disappear from an isolated joined node.
  • One capacitor initially has negative stored energy. — Stored capacitor energy depends on voltage squared and is nonnegative.
  • The capacitors cease having capacitance during the connection. — Their geometry and capacitance remain defined.

E1=D/(κ1ε0),V1=E1fdE_1=D/(\kappa_1\varepsilon_0),\quad V_1=E_1fdE1​=D/(κ1​ε0​),V1​=E1​fd

  2. State the result.

Answer: 3.37143×10−10 F3.37143\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm F3.37143×10−10F

Situation 59: Two dielectric layers through the gap · Find the voltage across dielectric 1

A parallel-plate capacitor has area 0.025 m² and total gap 0.0018 m. Dielectric 1 of relative permittivity 2 fills fraction 0.4 of the gap thickness. Dielectric 2 of relative permittivity 5 fills the remaining thickness. Each layer covers the whole plate area. An ideal 150 V source stays connected. Ignore fringing and free charge at the dielectric interface. Use ε0=8.85×10−12 F m−1\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}ε0​=8.85×10−12Fm−1. Find the voltage across dielectric 1.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. The field crosses both layers consecutively. They form series capacitances with the same free-charge magnitude per area.

  2. Add the two thickness-dependent inverse capacitances.

C=ε0Ad[f/κ1+(1−f)/κ2]=3.84115×10−10 FC=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d[f/\kappa_1+(1-f)/\kappa_2]}=3.84115\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm FC=d[f/κ1​+(1−f)/κ2​]ε0​A​=3.84115×10−10F
  1. Find the common free-charge surface density.
D=Q/A=CV/A=2.30469×10−6 C m−2D=Q/A=CV/A=2.30469\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}D=Q/A=CV/A=2.30469×10−6Cm−2

E1=D/(κ1ε0),V1=E1fdE_1=D/(\kappa_1\varepsilon_0),\quad V_1=E_1fdE1​=D/(κ1​ε0​),V1​=E1​fd
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
V1=E1fd=130208(0.4)(0.0018)V_1=E_1fd=130208(0.4)(0.0018)V1​=E1​fd=130208(0.4)(0.0018)

  1. Check the physical result. The two layer voltages add to the maintained source voltage.

93.75 V93.75\,\mathrm V93.75V

Answer: 93.75 V93.75\,\mathrm V93.75V

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 150 V150\,\mathrm V150V — The source voltage divides between both layers.
  • 60 V60\,\mathrm V60V — Thickness fraction alone does not set voltage fraction when fields differ.
  • 234.375 V234.375\,\mathrm V234.375V — This uses the whole gap rather than layer 1’s thickness.

Situation 60: Two dielectric layers through the gap · model check

A parallel-plate capacitor has area 0.025 m² and total gap 0.0018 m. Dielectric 1 of relative permittivity 2 fills fraction 0.4 of the gap thickness. Dielectric 2 of relative permittivity 5 fills the remaining thickness. Each layer covers the whole plate area. An ideal 150 V source stays connected. Ignore fringing and free charge at the dielectric interface. Use ε0=8.85×10−12 F m−1\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}ε0​=8.85×10−12Fm−1. What identifies this geometry as a series arrangement?

  1. Identify what stays fixed. The field crosses both layers consecutively. They form series capacitances with the same free-charge magnitude per area.

  2. Add the two thickness-dependent inverse capacitances.

C=ε0Ad[f/κ1+(1−f)/κ2]=3.84115×10−10 FC=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d[f/\kappa_1+(1-f)/\kappa_2]}=3.84115\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm FC=d[f/κ1​+(1−f)/κ2​]ε0​A​=3.84115×10−10F
  1. Find the common free-charge surface density.
D=Q/A=CV/A=2.30469×10−6 C m−2D=Q/A=CV/A=2.30469\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}D=Q/A=CV/A=2.30469×10−6Cm−2
  1. Recover each layer’s field and voltage.
E1=D/(κ1ε0),V1=E1fdE_1=D/(\kappa_1\varepsilon_0),\quad V_1=E_1fdE1​=D/(κ1​ε0​),V1​=E1​fd
  1. Apply the conclusion. The layer voltage drops add, while the free-charge magnitude is common.

Answer: A normal field path crosses dielectric 1 and then dielectric 2 through the plate gap.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Both dielectrics have equal voltage because each covers the whole area. — Equal area does not make stacked thickness layers parallel.
  • The larger dielectric constant removes all field from its layer. — A finite dielectric constant reduces the field but does not generally make it zero.
  • The source fixes the same field in every dielectric. — The source fixes total voltage; the layer fields depend on permittivity.
